content_voiceover: Let's walk through the standard pretransfusion testing algorithm, a must-know for boards. Step one: ABO and Rh typing is performed on both the patient and all candidate donor units. Step two: an antibody screen is run, mixing patient serum against a panel of reagent screening cells that carry clinically significant antigens. If the antibody screen is negative, you proceed directly to crossmatch using an abbreviated method, either immediate spin or a computer crossmatch, since a negative screen makes clinically significant incompatibility very unlikely. If the antibody screen is positive, you cannot skip ahead, you must first perform antibody identification using a full antigen panel of reagent red cells to determine antibody specificity. Only after identifying the antibody or antibodies do you proceed to full crossmatch, patient serum against donor cells, and where indicated, confirm the corresponding antigen is negative on the donor unit. This positive versus negative antibody screen branch point is the key decision node tested repeatedly on transfusion medicine boards.
keypoints: Workflow: ABO/Rh typing on patient and donor, then antibody screen
Negative antibody screen leads to an abbreviated crossmatch (immediate spin or computer method)
Positive antibody screen requires antibody identification via panel cells before crossmatch
Crossmatch may include confirming the donor unit is negative for the identified antigen
keypoint_voiceover: The pretransfusion algorithm: type patient and donor, then run an antibody screen. A negative screen lets you go straight to an abbreviated crossmatch. A positive screen means you must identify the antibody with panel cells first, then perform a full crossmatch, confirming the donor is negative for that antigen. Know this branch point cold for boards.
